u01s1l1: Hevalo, the deer who is your guide, leads you to a blue gate, where a man with a black moustache gives you a red apple. You take a bite, and Hevalo eats the rest.
u01s1l2: “Ez Hamo me,” says the man, and offers apple after apple, then teaches you how to refuse: “Na, spas.” When one drops on his head, Hamo rubs it: “Ez baş im!”
u01s1l3: At the gate you have your first talk: Hamo asks how you are, and you ask him back. Then he asks Hevalo, who has an apple in each cheek and only crunches.
u01s1l4: Hamo goes over it all with you at the gate: hello, how are you, yes thanks, no thanks. By the end you can answer him without stopping to think.
u01s2l1: Under the oldest apple tree Hamo brings a tray: tea, warm bread, spring water, and milk for Hevalo, who drinks it loudly.
u01s2l2: Hamo turns the tray into a game, “Ev çi ye?”, and you name the tea, the bread, the water. Whatever you name, Hamo calls it xweş: nice.
u01s2l3: Hamo runs back to the blue gate to welcome you properly, with a bow: “Bi xêr hatî!” Then comes the tea, very hot, with warm bread.
u01s2l4: Hamo welcomes you once more, and this time your answer is ready: “Xêra Xwedê li we bê!” Then he pours, and you name the tray.
u01s3l1: “Navê min Hamo ye,” he says, and at last asks your name. He writes it in the dust with a stick so as not to forget it, and Hevalo rubs it out with a hoof.
u01s3l2: Hamo shows you round: the gate creaks and the kitchen door sticks. Hevalo waits by the one door that stays shut, the apple store.
u01s3l3: You ask Hamo the Kurdish for everything, and he knows it all until you point at an old tool over the stove: “Ez nizanim!” Then Hevalo knocks over your tea.
u01s3l4: Hamo plays guess-who with you round the photos on his wall: “Ev kî ye?” Some faces you know; for the rest there is always “Ez nizanim.”
u01s4l1: At supper you ask for bread: “Ez nan dixwazim.” Hevalo asks for apples, as always: “Ez sêvan dixwazim!” And for both of you Hamo has two words: “Bixwe, vexwe!”
u01s4l2: The apple basket is empty, and a certain deer is lying very still under the table. But the water is cold, the tea is hot, and Hamo, who has a whole orchard, laughs.
u01s4l3: Hamo says “Şev baş!” at the guest-room door, and the next morning he is at the gate with tea: “Roj baş!” Ten steps down the lane, Hevalo turns back for an apple.
u01s4l4: On a morning walk with Hevalo you say hello and goodbye to half the village. At the blue gate Hamo has tea and news: the neighbours are coming tomorrow.
u02s1l1: Hamo shows you the photos on his wall: his father and mother, far away in Kobanî. Then a boy looks in at the door: Nazê’s son.
u02s1l2: The next photo shows all four children in a row: Hamo, his brother and his two sisters. “Em malbatek in,” he says proudly, and straightens every frame, twice.
u02s1l3: Xezo, the young teacher from Amed, comes to the gate, and everyone says who they are: Hamo a man, Xezo a woman, Hevalo an animal.
u02s1l4: Hamo shows the neighbours his photos. Baran finds Hamo at ten, with no moustache, so Hamo stands up straight: “Ez mêr im.”
u02s2l1: Hamo introduces Nazê’s children, her son Baran and her daughter Hêvî. Then they count the hens, who will not stand still.
u02s2l2: Dapîr Şemsê counts three hens, Hêvî four, and Hamo five, because he counted Hevalo. Then Hamo asks Baran how his grandfather is, in the next village.
u02s2l3: Round the tea tray Hêvî holds up six fingers, and Hevalo, says Hamo, is five, or eats like five deer. Then Hamo counts Dapîr’s children and runs out of fingers.
u02s2l4: Dapîr and Hêvî count the hens again and finally agree. Then Hêvî counts Hamo’s family on her fingers, and Hamo helps her.
u02s3l1: The neighbours come back for breakfast on a cloth on the floor. Hamo boils an egg for everyone, and one more for Hevalo, who never eats them.
u02s3l2: Baran says he is nine, nearly ten, so not a child. Hamo just pushes the milk and the yoghurt towards him: “Şîr vexwe, mast bixwe!”
u02s3l3: Nazê made the bread, and Hamo teaches you what to say to her: “Destê te sax be!” You are thirsty, and every time you say thank you, he fills your glass again.
u02s3l4: Breakfast again, this time on a cloth in the yard. You thank Nazê properly, and Hamo says “Noşî can be!” to everyone who takes a bite.
u02s4l1: Everyone says which animals they have: Nazê a cat, Dapîr hens and a goat, and Hamo Şêro the dog and Bozo the donkey, who puts his big grey head over the wall.
u02s4l2: Nazê brings a pot of her cooking, and Hamo praises it to the whole table. Little Hêvî sits with Hevalo, and Hamo takes five sugars.
u02s4l3: At supper Hamo passes round the bread: “Kerem bike!” Hêvî counts to ten without a mistake, and while you tell Hamo where you are from, Hevalo eats your bread.
u02s4l4: A game at supper: everyone says one thing they have and one thing they don’t. Nazê has a cat; Hamo has a dog and a donkey.
u03s1l1: Hamo shows you round his house: a big room, a small window, a low table and four chairs. Hevalo checks every chair for an apple, and finds one.
u03s1l2: In every room something is in the wrong place: a hen on the bedding, a shoe on the table. Hamo carries the hen out to the cat.
u03s1l3: Up on the flat roof, where everyone sleeps in summer, Hamo sits you down with tea and tenûr bread. On the table is a map of Sêvan, and Hevalo sniffs it for apples.
u03s1l4: Hamo takes you round the house once more, faster: a room, a window, the roof, the tenûr. Then he finds his own house on the map of Sêvan and taps it.
u03s2l1: In Hamo’s orchard the apples are red and the gate is blue. Red is the best colour in the world, Hamo declares, and Hevalo votes for red by eating one.
u03s2l2: Sêvan has a hundred yellow flowers and a hundred old doors. Hamo shows you his new door, which already looks old, and Hevalo eats three yellow flowers.
u03s2l3: “Binêre!” Hamo points at Dapîr’s goat, white from her ears to her long beard. Then she starts on Dapîr’s flowers, and Hamo saves them with a piece of bread.
u03s2l4: You name the colours of Sêvan: the blue gate, the red apples, the white goat. Then you find fresh yellow paint on the window. Who could it be?
u03s3l1: Hamo looks for his cap on the table, under the bed, under the walnut tree. Then Hêvî points: it is on his head.
u03s3l2: In Hêvî’s game Hamo calls out eyes, ears, head, and everyone touches them, Hevalo with his nose. You wash your hands, and hot bread comes out of the tenûr.
u03s3l3: Under the walnut tree Hamo shares an apple: half for you, half for him. But his half is gone: Hevalo’s nose is behind the tree, and the apple is in his mouth.
u03s3l4: Lunch is ready, but where is everyone? Şêro is under the table, the cat is in the yard, and Hevalo’s nose is behind the tree again. You find them all with Hamo.
u03s4l1: Hamo shows you the school, where Xezo from Amed teaches; the shop, never open when you need it; and the spring, so cold that Hevalo drinks with his eyes shut.
u03s4l2: From the roof you see the mountain, the town below, the sheep of Bişar the shepherd and Ferhad’s cow. Then the sun goes down behind the mountain.
u03s4l3: On the roof in the evening, as the birds sing in the apple trees, Hamo has news: tomorrow is market day in town! Hevalo cannot keep still: the town has new apples.
u03s4l4: At sunset you name the village from the roof: the school, the shop, the spring, the mountain. Xezo waves from the school door.
u04s1l1: Market day, and you are coming too. Bozo carries the empty baskets and stops at every flower. He is admiring the view, says Hamo, who stops at every neighbour.
u04s1l2: On the way Hamo names all he sees, the river, the mountain, a hen, so fast that you ask: “Tu çi dibêjî?”
u04s1l3: Hamo knows every seller, and Mîrza best of all. He tells Mîrza that you speak Kurdish, while Hevalo stands very still by the apples: only looking, for now.
u04s1l4: Hamo shows you round the market: Mîrza is selling, the baker is shouting, Bozo is eating a seller’s blue flowers, and Hevalo has not moved from Mîrza’s apples.
u04s2l1: At the stall Hamo asks for tomatoes and potatoes, and the seller asks what he wants to eat this week. Fruit, says Hamo, eyeing the apples; Hevalo eyes them too.
u04s2l2: Hamo says he can carry everything and can tell a fresh fish by its eyes. He gives the bags to Bozo, and when a fish looks back at him, he buys some meat as well.
u04s2l3: Hamo takes three spoonfuls of sugar in Mîrza’s tea, then a fourth: “Zêde!” cries Mîrza. Hamo asks how you take yours, then adds two spoonfuls to it himself.
u04s2l4: Lunch at the market: bread, cheese and very sweet tea. Hevalo says he is not hungry, but his nose is right beside Mîrza’s apples.
u04s3l1: Hamo reads the prices aloud, shocked by each: twenty for grapes, thirty for a basket! “Hemû bi çend e?” he asks a seller, then counts his money three times.
u04s3l2: Hamo and Mîrza haggle over a basket of apples for ten minutes. In the end Hamo pays fifty and says it was cheap, and they both laugh.
u04s3l3: Grapes, onions and apples come to a hundred and ten. A thousand? cries Hamo, who was not listening. You are the guest, so he pays.
u04s3l4: Hamo adds it all up again and has twenty left, exactly the price of a glass of tea, so he spends it on tea. Mîrza’s tea is good, he says, and cheap.
u04s4l1: An apple basket is empty, and nobody knows who ate the apples. Bozo looks away, and Hevalo shakes his head very fast: “Ez nizanim! Ez hîç nizanim!”
u04s4l2: The basket is empty, but Hevalo’s belly is full. Is it true that he was by the basket? Hevalo says that is wrong, but there is apple peel on his nose.
u04s4l3: Hamo swears Hevalo never eats apples, but Hevalo has apple all over his face, so nobody believes Hamo and everyone laughs. Then Hamo’s phone rings: it is Nazê.
u04s4l4: Home at sunset, Bozo groaning under the bags. You go over the day: what you saw, what you bought, what it cost. Where is Hamo’s phone?
u05s1l1: Dapîr’s calendar hangs by the stove, and Hamo explains the week: it starts on Saturday, and this Saturday you all go to Kobanî.
u05s1l2: Baran reads on Monday and reads more on Tuesday. Hamo nods wisely: in his day they read under the walnut tree, so now he can only read in the shade.
u05s1l3: Hamo bakes bread on Wednesday, writes to his mother on Thursday, then asks how long you will stay in Sêvan. As long as there are apples, says Hevalo’s face.
u05s1l4: Everyone writes their week on Dapîr’s calendar: school for Baran, the tenûr for Dapîr, tea every day for Hamo. Then Dapîr circles Saturday in red, twice.
u05s2l1: Hamo names the months like old friends: Adar brings Newroz, and Nîsan the blossom on the apple trees. Friday is for tea.
u05s2l2: Nazê’s children both have birthdays coming: Baran in May and Hêvî in June. Hamo’s is in May too, but only his mother knows the day.
u05s2l3: It is your birthday, and Hamo is the first to wish you a happy one. His own? He can’t remember it, nor his age. Your present? Don’t worry, he remembers.
u05s2l4: Hamo and the children count the days to Saturday and the months to Newroz, and practise their birthday wishes for Baran’s in May.
u05s3l1: Hamo has three clocks, each telling a different time. He trusts none of them, only his phone, which says it is time for tea.
u05s3l2: Hamo wakes with the hens, gets up when the tea is ready and washes at the spring; after lunch he sleeps for “just five minutes”, which last an hour.
u05s3l3: Lunch is at noon, and Hamo arrives at one o’clock, delighted; Nazê laughs over the wall. Hamo is never late, he says: everyone else is just early.
u05s3l4: Hamo’s day runs from the hens at six to bed at eleven: tea, the orchard, more tea, lunch at noon for everyone else, and a nap of five minutes that lasts an hour.
u05s4l1: Hamo admits that he is sometimes late, and Nazê coughs; often late, and Dapîr coughs. Then he goes to work in the orchard.
u05s4l2: Baran explains the bus: it leaves the square at eight and waits for nobody. “Belê, belê,” says Hamo, already planning a glass of tea at five to eight.
u05s4l3: The bus leaves at eight sharp on Saturday, with no time for tea. Hamo gives his solemn word, “Soza min soz e!”: if the bus will not stop, he will run after it.
u05s4l4: Hamo wakes at half past eight. The bus pulls away just as you reach the square. The next one is in the evening: time for tea.
u06s1l1: Ferhad’s tractor takes everyone to the main road, where a minibus driver squeezes you all in, Hevalo too. The driver is fast: “Hêdî, hêdî!” says Hamo.
u06s1l2: Kobanî has grown since Hamo was a boy: he turns left every time a sign says right, and gets lost in his own town. Go straight on, he tells himself: “Here rasterast!”
u06s1l3: Kobanî at last, with its crowded market and Miştenûr hill high above the roofs. Hevalo climbs onto a flat roof for the view, and Hamo calls him down.
u06s1l4: Hevalo trots straight down the street to the house where Hamo grew up, with the old fig tree in the yard, and Hamo shows you every window and step.
u06s2l1: At his father’s house Hamo plays host at once: “Werin hundir! Rûnin!” he calls, and his sister’s children climb all over their uncle, their Xalo.
u06s2l2: At the table the orders never stop: “Bixwe! Vexwe! Bide min!” Hamo’s uncle and aunt bring more food, and he eats everything, and is given it all again.
u06s2l3: Şêro has come to Kobanî too, and he won’t hurt you, says Hamo. Four sugars? “Neke!” Off to the market? “Neçe!” Dinner is ready.
u06s2l4: After dinner Hamo brings out an old photo: his parents, his brother, his two sisters and himself. Careful: it is forty years old.
u06s3l1: Hamo lists what he must do in Kobanî: climb Miştenûr, buy his father a book, visit his aunt, take Hevalo along. Then he adds “drink tea” to every line.
u06s3l2: Who washes the dishes? Everyone should help, says Hamo’s mother, and every man in the room suddenly needs a rest.
u06s3l3: The bookseller is closing, but he opens the door again for five minutes, and Hamo buys a book of proverbs for his father, who is a book of proverbs himself.
u06s3l4: Hamo gives his father the book of proverbs, and his father knows half of them already. It is late, says Hamo’s mother; one more, says his father, and reads ten.
u06s4l1: The old baker remembers Hamo as the boy who ate the crusts on the way home. Back at the house, the children talk about trains and planes.
u06s4l2: Packing: a heap of shoes, bags and parcels. Hamo sorts it all out: this bag is his, that one is yours, and nothing belongs to Hevalo except the apples.
u06s4l3: On the last evening the news says snow is coming and the mountain road may close, so you must go back early: Hamo sets three alarms and asks you to check them.
u06s4l4: At dawn Hamo is on time, for once. His mother fills every bag with bread and cheese, the children shout goodbye, and the minibus climbs into the snow.
u07s1l1: On the road home snow is falling, and Hamo explains the weather to the driver: rain, snow, wind, sun. The driver already knew.
u07s1l2: Snowed in, Hamo tells the children about the seasons: winter is for soup and spring for roses. Hevalo fogs up the window, waiting for the warmth.
u07s1l3: A storm rattles the shutters as Hamo asks about the weather where you come from. Outside, Hevalo builds a snow-deer with an apple nose, then eats the nose.
u07s1l4: The sun is back, the snow melts and the stream by the walnut tree sings again. Hamo phones every neighbour with the news: Newroz is coming!
u07s2l1: Newroz is coming, and Hamo hands out the jobs: Baran will gather firewood, Nazê will sew clothes and Dapîr will bake. Hamo will light the fire, and supervise.
u07s2l2: The children count the days to Newroz, and Hamo’s great speech has gone missing. Bring it here, Hamo tells Hevalo, who is chewing something papery.
u07s2l3: Newroz is the new year, says Hamo, and he tells you the legend of Kawa the blacksmith, who rose against the tyrant Dehak and lit the fires.
u07s2l4: Hamo practises his Newroz speech on the hens, who leave, and on Bozo, who leaves too. Only you stay to the end.
u07s3l1: At the school Xezo teaches the children the govend, and Hamo tells you all about the drum and the zurna. Soon he joins the line himself.
u07s3l2: Nazê has sewn new clothes, and Hamo puts on his suit with the green sash at once, over his pyjamas. He will lead the govend, he says, if his knees agree.
u07s3l3: The night before Newroz, Hamo shows you a full moon and a thousand stars. Then a lamp glows at the gate: the neighbours have come for tea.
u07s3l4: The neighbours are at the table and the firewood is on the hill. Tomorrow Baran will play the drum, his uncle the zurna, and Hamo will lead the govend.
u07s4l1: The whole village picnics on the hill for Newroz. At dusk Hamo lights the fire, and everyone jumps over it for good health, Hamo holding his moustache.
u07s4l2: By the dying fire Hamo tries a shepherd’s flute. His first squeak sends Hevalo bolting, and everyone laughs until tears of joy come.
u07s4l3: The morning after the govend, Hamo cannot get out of bed: “Pişta min diêşe!” His back is very bad, he says, and he asks for tea, honey and sympathy, in that order.
u07s4l4: From his bed Hamo tells everyone about Newroz: the fire, the flute, the speech that Hevalo ate. When Nazê phones, he says his back is a little better.
u08s1l1: Hamo lies in bed and lists everything that hurts, from his legs to his shoulders. Rest, says Nazê, but Hamo has been resting since breakfast, and it is exhausting.
u08s1l2: Hamo has a sore neck, a cough and probably a fever, and he is very sad until he hears the doctor is coming. Then he hides the honey and looks almost cheerful.
u08s1l3: At the word “hospital” Hamo sits up: he does not want to go! Then his tooth hurts, and his chest. Healthy, says Doctor Azad: he just talks a lot.
u08s1l4: A week in bed, and Hamo is already planning next Newroz. All that is wrong with him now, says Doctor Azad, is his impatience.
u08s2l1: Doctor Azad listens to Hamo’s heart and presses his back. Pills, please, not the needle, says Hamo; the doctor laughs: he will be better in a week.
u08s2l2: Walk every day, says the doctor, and no honey at night. Then the neighbours bring honey, and he gives every jar to you to guard.
u08s2l3: In the morning a honey jar is empty and Hamo’s moustache is sticky. Hamo swears he is innocent; Hevalo, who for once is innocent, looks offended.
u08s2l4: The honey case is closed: one look at Hamo’s sticky moustache was enough. From now on you and Hevalo guard the jars, and Hamo is better, but sad.
u08s3l1: Back on his feet, Hamo compares everyone: who is taller, who is older, who is cleverer. The cleverest, he says, is Hamo.
u08s3l2: Hamo asks everyone their favourite season, fruit and place; Hevalo’s answer is always the same. Hamo’s is his biggest tea glass.
u08s3l3: At the tea house contest Ferhad’s moustache is longer, but everyone agrees Hamo’s is the most beautiful. Hamo promises Ferhad the prize next year.
u08s3l4: Every day Hamo walks with you up to the hill where the Newroz fire burned. The best medicine, he says, is mountain air, and tea.
u08s4l1: Baran comes home late one evening, muddy to the knees, and says nothing. Hêvî is amazed that her brother is so quiet; Hamo has a feeling, and will wait.
u08s4l2: Baran sits alone on the flat roof. Hamo climbs up, sits beside him, and talks quietly about trust: a secret kept alone only grows.
u08s4l3: At eight, Hamo tells you, he lost the neighbour’s best ram and hid all day, afraid to go home. That evening he told the truth, and was called brave.
u08s4l4: A storm is coming. At last Baran comes in and sits by the stove, but he will not tell yet. Hevalo gives him his last apple.
u09s1l1: At breakfast Baran takes a deep breath, and the table goes quiet: yesterday he went to the river with Bozo, and something happened.
u09s1l2: Baran goes on: Bozo saw a goat across the valley and ran, and Baran ran after him over the stones and along the cliffs. He never caught him, and was left all alone.
u09s1l3: Baran was a little afraid, he admits: he sat down under a walnut tree to think, and fell asleep. Hamo says that he himself would have eaten some walnuts first.
u09s1l4: Baran followed the stars home, not afraid at all, he says, and found Bozo eating Dapîr’s mint. But on the way he saw smoke from a tent where nobody lives.
u09s2l1: Hamo strokes his moustache and remembers being a boy, and then a handsome young man in the traditional suit. The summers were longer then, says Dapîr.
u09s2l2: When it gets dark, wolves roam round the village, says Hamo. But the wolf at the gate one night was no wolf: it was the neighbours’ dog.
u09s2l3: A boy on a mule brings a message from Bişar the shepherd: every night something wild and shy, like a deer, comes to his tent. Hevalo’s ears shoot up.
u09s2l4: Everyone tells a story with an animal in it, Hêvî with a clever fox. The best is Dapîr’s true story, of a lamb she found in the snow and carried home.
u09s3l1: Hamo shows Baran how to tell a story in order: first, then, in the end. Baran wants the end at once. Be patient, says Hamo: first tea, then the story.
u09s3l2: Hamo retells Baran’s day as a hero’s journey: Baran walked, wandered and laughed at his fear. A bird flew over him, an eagle, says Hamo; a crow, says Dapîr.
u09s3l3: Hamo decides that this summer everyone goes up to Bişar’s tent on the zozan. The packing begins at once, and Bozo, hearing the word “zozan”, runs away again.
u09s3l4: Packing for the zozan: tents, ropes and four baskets of apples, for Bişar, says Hamo, while Hevalo says nothing. Only Bozo is cross: he does not want to go.
u09s4l1: Dapîr packs her saddlebags and tells you about her youth: her family had a horse, and she rode it up to the pastures and came down the mountain singing.
u09s4l2: The last time they moved, Hamo was a whole day late, by mistake. Tomorrow at dawn he will be wide awake, he says, and Bozo watches shyly from behind a rock.
u09s4l3: Hevalo follows Bozo’s tracks to the spring, and there is Bozo with Ferhad’s little donkey, refusing to come home. “Bozo evîndar e!” says Hamo, delighted.
u09s4l4: On the climb Dapîr shows you the rock where they rested and the spring where she filled her jug. Then sheep fill the path.
u10s1l1: Bişar, Hamo’s old friend, meets everyone on the path. Over tea on the rocks he asks what you saw, what you ate and what Bozo did, and Hamo tells it all, twice.
u10s1l2: Bişar asks what everyone saw on the climb: Baran an eagle, Hêvî flowers, Hamo nothing, as he was talking. Dapîr gives Hevalo an apple.
u10s1l3: At dusk a doe comes for Bişar’s salt and looks straight at Hevalo, who drops his apple. “Bêdeng!” whispers Hamo, and he leaves a sack of apples by the tent.
u10s1l4: By the fire Bişar says the doe comes every night for the salt, and Hamo names her Zerê, “the golden one”. By morning Hevalo is gone, and so is the sack of apples.
u10s2l1: Dawn on the zozan: Bişar teaches you to milk a ewe, and Hamo proudly spills half his milk. Dapîr rocks the goatskin churn until only the ayran is left.
u10s2l2: Dapîr and Nazê bake bread on the saj, each one thin as paper, and Hamo “helps” and burns one. Then you catch Hevalo slipping off with an apple: “Min tu dîtî!”
u10s2l3: The tracks of two deer lead to a hidden lake, where Hevalo and Zerê share apples, and to a ruined stone house. Who was its owner? Hamo asks you to guess.
u10s2l4: Back at the tents everyone tells what they saw at the lake, over Nazê’s thin bread. Then they sing and dance the govend.
u10s3l1: At the old stone house Dapîr stops: it was her family’s summer home. She used to swim in the lake, make dried curd on that very roof and look after the lambs.
u10s3l2: When Dapîr was a girl, the household slept on felt rugs by the fire, and every evening a young man from Kobanî used to play the flute by the lake.
u10s3l3: The last day on the zozan. Zerê is gone into the grass, everyone packs with a heavy heart, and Bişar says: until next summer.
u10s3l4: On the last evening Dapîr hums the flute player’s tune by the fire, and nobody says much. Tomorrow at dawn the whole camp goes down to the village.
u10s4l1: Back in Sêvan, Hamo shows the neighbours his photos of the summer, mostly of his finger. The biggest event was Hevalo’s love: say “Zerê”, and his ears go up.
u10s4l2: On the first night, Baran reminds everyone, Hamo saw two bright eyes by the salt and called them “just a goat”. Hamo is astonished.
u10s4l3: Hamo writes the summer down in his old notebook, looking so worried that you ask if he is ill. No: the apples are nearly ripe.
u10s4l4: Hamo reads the summer aloud from his notebook, and everyone has something to correct. The bread? Hamo burned it, not Bişar.
u11s1l1: September, and the apples are nearly ripe. Hamo shows you the village trades: the farmer, the worker, the cook, the builder. Each says his own is the best.
u11s1l2: The children play “what will you be?”: Baran a writer, Hêvî a nurse for the hens. Ferhad brings saplings, and Hamo says he will plant them, looking at you.
u11s1l3: News in the village: a big school in Hewlêr has offered Xezo a post. An honour for Sêvan, Hamo says over tea, but you point out that Hewlêr is far.
u11s1l4: Hamo works in the orchard all day, and Ferhad, Mîrza and Bişar stop by, each sure his own work is the best. Hamo agrees with them all, and all go home happy.
u11s2l1: The harvest begins, and Hamo has a plan: ladders on the left, baskets on the right, tea in the middle. Dapîr, the most experienced, says nothing and keeps picking.
u11s2l2: Everyone picks, Hamo singing at the top of a ladder, until Bozo’s load is so heavy that he sits down. Then a cloud comes over the mountain, and everyone hurries.
u11s2l3: After the harvest the village meets. Ferhad wants every house to plant saplings, and Xezo says she will go to Hewlêr in the spring, and come back every Newroz.
u11s2l4: Xezo writes to the school in Hewlêr: yes, she will come in the spring. Mîrza takes the letter to the post, so the whole village knows by lunchtime.
u11s3l1: Xezo has set Baran’s class a task: a talk about Sêvan in front of the whole school. Baran is shy and his voice shakes. That is why, says Hamo, they will practise.
u11s3l2: Baran lists his fears: the hall is big, the children will laugh, his voice will shake. Hamo’s advice: speak slowly and forget nothing, as he does in his own speeches.
u11s3l3: Hamo helps Baran write his talk, letter by letter. Baran practises in front of the hens, and Hevalo, the most patient listener in the world, stamps a hoof in applause.
u11s3l4: Baran gives his talk in the school hall: Sêvan, its apples, its people, and Hevalo. Xezo says it was the best talk of the year, and Baran gives it again at home, twice.
u11s4l1: Hamo asks everyone their goals: Hêvî wants a cat, Nazê wants Hamo on time for once, and Hamo wants a new tea glass. Learning, he tells you, is one step at a time.
u11s4l2: Xezo will teach children their mother tongue in Hewlêr. Hamo remembers his first winter here, far from Kobanî: he was homesick, and the village gave him warmth.
u11s4l3: The first snow. Hamo lights the stove and promises an evening of tales every night, each one of Dapîr’s. He asks which you like better, a tale or a song.
u11s4l4: Snow on every roof, and Xezo’s last winter in Sêvan. The neighbours crowd round Hamo’s stove, and he puts the tea on: the tales begin tomorrow.
u12s1l1: Hamo begins the first tale: a mother goat tells her two kids, Şengê and Pengê, never to open the door. But the wolf is a liar, and makes his voice as soft as wool.
u12s1l2: The wolf knocks and sings like the kids’ mother. Clever Şengê sees through the trick: the paw under the door is black.
u12s1l3: The children turn the tale into a play by the stove. Hevalo gets the wolf and plays it terribly, far too friendly, pushing apples under the door with his hoof.
u12s1l4: Dapîr takes her spoon out of her tea: every tale, she says, is a piece of advice. Baran asks for another, and then, in the middle of a snowy night, someone knocks.
u12s2l1: A knock at midnight in deep snow: an old dengbêj and his grandson. Hamo spreads the meal cloth at once, and when they praise Sêvan, he pretends not to be pleased.
u12s2l2: Over dinner everyone talks at once: the old dengbêj asks whether they can leave in February, and Baran wants a play tonight.
u12s2l3: After dinner the old dengbêj sings kilams of the old days. His last is about a shepherd who played the flute by a lake, but its last verse is lost.
u12s2l4: Hamo phones the town to ask whether the pass is open, but nobody answers. When the snow stops the guests leave, and the whole village hums the unfinished song.
u12s3l1: The second night’s tale: the fox and the bear share a field, and the bear always gets the tasteless half. He sulks so loudly that Hevalo hides behind the stove.
u12s3l2: Dapîr answers every tale with a proverb, Hamo every proverb with a tale: drop by drop, water becomes a lake; a sweet tongue brings the snake out of its hole.
u12s3l3: A proverb duel, with Hamo as judge: you bring a problem, and Dapîr has a proverb for every one. Hevalo’s answer is an apple.
u12s3l4: Hamo’s phone rings: a call from Kobanî, the town where he grew up. Everyone shouts a proverb down the line, and Dapîr, as always, has the last word.
u12s4l1: Spring, and Ferhad’s son’s wedding fills the field below the village: the big drum, the joyful cries. Hamo leads the govend.
u12s4l2: Xezo makes her goodbye speech: thank you for every tale and every glass of tea. “Ez ê bêriya we hemûyan bikim,” she says, then turns to Hamo and cannot finish.
u12s4l3: Dawn at the blue gate, and the bus is waiting for Xezo. Hamo wishes her a safe journey, and she orders him to drink his tea with less sugar. Hevalo gets the last apple.
u12s4l4: The bus has gone, and the village turns to you: your road is ending too. Everyone blesses you at the blue gate, and Hamo shows you the sapling he planted for you.
